Smarter rivals: airlines that plan routes, price them and feel your competition

November 11, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

The AI airlines got a new way of deciding. We ran the old one through thirty years of simulated play and found it withdrew two of every three routes it launched within a year, took delivery of "new" aircraft whose production lines had closed decades ago, opened hubs in other countries, and never changed a fare. This applies to new games. A game you have already started keeps the rivals it started with.

  • They look before they launch. A rival now costs a route on its own books before opening it: the aircraft, the schedule and who already flies the pair. A route that would lose money is not opened. Fewer than one launch in ten is now withdrawn within a year, and the News tab is much quieter for it.
  • Aircraft that suit the route. A thin short route gets a regional aircraft, a busy one a big narrow-body and a dense long-haul route a wide-body. Rivals order types that are still being built, so no more premium airlines on fleets of Il-86s, and nothing bigger than a narrow-body flies under 1,500 km. Each airline leans towards Airbus or Boeing, and Russian and Chinese types stay with the airlines that would really buy them. See the aircraft guide for the types.
  • They stay at home. A rival bases its aircraft in its own country, and every route it opens has one end there. European airlines treat the single market as home, as the real low-cost carriers do. Second hubs are opened at home too.
  • Fares move. A route that keeps selling out is priced up before more flights are added, and further where the rival has the pair to itself. A soft route is priced down. A rival with a monopoly and high fares is an invitation.
  • They feel you. A rival's passengers on a pair you share now depend on what each of you offers: departures, fare and quality. Out-fly or undercut a rival and its income on that route really falls, until it trims, cuts fares or leaves. Sell out your own flights and the rival picks up some of the passengers you turn away. Before, a rival's books split a pair evenly whatever anyone did. The competition guide has more.
  • Regional airports. Rivals now serve the regional airports of their home market, not only the big ones. A profitable regional route you have to yourself may not stay that way.
  • Old fleets cost money. Rival aircraft now age, and maintenance climbs with age. A healthy rival replaces a fleet at around 14 years. A struggling one keeps flying old aircraft and pays more every year.
  • A second chance, then a sale. The first time an established rival fails it restructures: it drops its loss-making routes and flies on with lower costs for three years. A second failure closes it, and its aircraft go on a liquidation sale at the top of the Competition tab for eight weeks. Each is sold at its book value and joins your fleet the week you buy it, with no wait for a delivery slot.
  • About as rich as before. An airline that stops wasting money gets richer, so rival costs were raised to match. In our test worlds the rivals end ten years with the same average market value as they did before, and networks the same size. They are harder to push around, not wealthier.
